scenes.title:
The Files API
[[Upload once, use everywhere]]
scenes.subtitle: Stop sending the same PDF to Claude with every request

lines.say: Every time your app asks Claude about a PDF, it sends the whole file again. Every question, every time.
The Files API fixes that. In this video, you'll learn what it is, how it works, and when to use it.
Then we'll upload a real PDF, use it in Python, step by step, and clean up after ourselves.

scenes.heading: What is the [[Files API]]?
items: **Upload** a file once, get back a **file ID**
Use that ID in **any message**, as often as you like

lines.say: So, what is the Files API?
It lets you upload a file to Anthropic once. You get back a file ID, a short name for that file.
Then you use that ID in your messages, as many times as you like, instead of sending the file again.
Think of a library card number. You don't carry the book around: you just give the number.
And you can list your files, check them, and delete them when you're done.

scenes.heading: Upload, [[reference]], manage

rows.label: Upload
rows.text: Send the file once → get a **file_id**

rows.label: Reference
rows.text: A **document** or **image** block with the file_id

scenes.banner: File operations are free; the content still counts as input tokens

lines.say: Here's how it works, in three parts.
Upload: you send the file once, and the API gives you a file ID. Files can be up to five hundred megabytes each.
Reference: in a message, you add a document block for a PDF or a text file, or an image block for a picture, with the file ID as the source.
Manage: you can list your files, get their details, and delete them. Or set an expiration when you upload, and they disappear on their own.
Uploading, listing and deleting are free. But when a message uses the file, its content still counts as input tokens, like before.

left.title: Use it when…
left.body:
• The same file is used
  in many requests
• Large PDFs and images
• Datasets for the code
  execution tool
• Agents with many steps

right.title: Skip it when…
right.body:
• A short text, used once:
  just paste it in
• Word or Excel files:
  .docx / .xlsx aren't read
  as documents. Convert
  them to text first

lines.say: When should you use it?
When the same file is used in many requests: large PDFs and images, datasets for the code execution tool, or agents that work in many steps.
Skip it for a short text you use once: just paste it into the message. And Word or Excel files aren't read as documents. Convert them to text first.

scenes.heading: The [[Maple Mugs]] handbook, as a PDF

left.title: Without the Files API
left.body:
Every question sends
the whole PDF again:
120,004 characters

✗ Every time

right.title: With the Files API
right.body:
Upload the PDF once

Every question sends
a short file ID

✓ "file_011CUz4m..."

lines.say: Our use case: the Maple Mugs help desk from my last videos. This time, the store handbook is a three-page PDF.
Without the Files API, every question sends the whole PDF again: more than a hundred and twenty thousand characters.
With the Files API, we upload it once. Every question just sends a short file ID.
Here's our folder, with the handbook PDF, and a script that asks Claude about it the usual way.

do.text:
"""Asks about the handbook by sending the whole PDF every time."""
import base64
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
data = Path("handbook.pdf").read_bytes()
pdf = base64.standard_b64encode(data).decode()
print(f"Sending {len(pdf):,} characters of PDF data...")

reply = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=300,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "document", "source": {
            "type": "base64", "media_type": "application/pdf",
            "data": pdf}},
        {"type": "text", "text": sys.argv[1]},
    ]}],
)
print(reply.content[0].text)

lines.say: It reads the PDF, turns it into base64 text, and puts all of it into the message.
Let's ask two questions.

do.text: python no_files.py "Are your mugs dishwasher safe?"
out: Yes! All our mugs are dishwasher and microwave safe. They're not oven safe, though.
Standard US shipping is free on orders over $60. Otherwise it's $6.

lines.say: Both answers are right. But each question sent the whole file again. With a big PDF, or many users, that's a lot of data going back and forth, for nothing.
Step one: upload the PDF.
I open the file, and call files dot upload, with three things: the file name, the file itself, and its type, application slash PDF.

do.text:
"""Uploads the handbook PDF once and saves its file ID."""
from pathlib import Path

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

# 1. Upload once: file name, file, type
with open("handbook.pdf", "rb") as f:
    uploaded = client.files.upload(
        file=("handbook.pdf", f, "application/pdf"),
        expires_in_seconds=30 * 24 * 3600,  # deleted after 30 days
    )

# 2. Keep the ID: it's all you need from now on
Path("file_id.txt").write_text(uploaded.id)
print(f"Uploaded {uploaded.filename}: {uploaded.size_bytes:,} bytes")
print(f"file_id: {uploaded.id}")

lines.say: The expiration is optional. Here, the file deletes itself after thirty days. You can choose anything from one hour to ninety days.
Then I save the file ID. That ID is all we need from now on.
Let's run it, once.
Uploaded: ninety kilobytes, and here's our file ID. It starts with file, underscore.
Step two: use the file ID.
This script reads the saved ID, and asks Claude a question about the handbook.

do.text:
"""Asks a question about the handbook, using its file ID."""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
file_id = Path("file_id.txt").read_text().strip()

reply = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=300,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        # The PDF by reference: nothing is uploaded again
        {"type": "document",
         "source": {"type": "file", "file_id": file_id}},
        {"type": "text", "text": sys.argv[1]},
    ]}],
)
print(reply.content[0].text)

lines.say: Here's the key part: a document block, whose source has type file, and our file ID. No base64, no file. Just the ID.
The question goes after the document, in a normal text block.
Step three: ask again, as many times as you like.
Same two questions as before.

do.text: python ask.py "Are your mugs dishwasher safe?"
out: Yes! All our mugs are dishwasher and microwave safe. They're not oven safe, though.
Standard US shipping is free on orders over $60. Otherwise it's $6.

lines.say: Same correct answers. But this time, each request only sent the file ID. The PDF was uploaded once, and it stays there.
One thing doesn't change: Claude still reads the PDF, so its content is billed as input tokens on every question. To pay less for that, combine it with prompt caching, from my last video.
Step four: list and delete.
This small script lists your files. Or, with delete and a file ID, removes one.
Let's list them.
There's our handbook. When we're done with it, we delete it.
Gone. Deleted files can't be recovered, so delete only what you no longer need.
The files also include an offline test, so you can try everything with no API key.

cards.title: Can't edit a file
cards.text: Upload a new one, **delete** the old one

cards.title: Add prompt caching
cards.text: The content is still billed as input tokens

lines.say: Four tips.
One: files belong to your whole workspace. Any API key in it can use any file. So never accept a file ID from your users. Keep track of which file belongs to whom in your own app.
Two: set an expiration for temporary files, so you don't pile up old ones.
Three: files can't be edited or renamed. To change one, upload a new file and delete the old one.
And four: the content still counts as input tokens. For a file you reuse a lot, add prompt caching.

scenes.heading: Recap
items: Use it in a **document** or **image** block

lines.say: Let's recap.
Upload a file once with files dot upload, and keep its file ID.
Use the ID in a document block or an image block, in as many messages as you like.
And when you're done, delete it, or let it expire.
